statement.title: A. Maximize?
statement.legend:
You are given an integer $x$. Your task is to find any integer $y$ $(1\le y \lt x)$ such that $\gcd(x,y)+y$ is maximum possible.

Note that if there is more than one $y$ which satisfies the statement, you are allowed to find any.

$\gcd(a,b)$ is the Greatest Common Divisor of $a$ and $b$. For example, $\gcd(6,4)=2$.
statement.input_spec:
The first line contains a single integer $t$ ($1 \le t \le 1000$) — the number of test cases.

Each of the following $t$ lines contains a single integer $x$ ($2 \le x \le 1000$).
statement.output_spec: For each test case, output any $y$ ($1 \le y  \lt  x$), which satisfies the statement.

editorial.tutorial:
The core idea is to find the upper bound of $\gcd(x,y)+y$.

Let us look closer at the formula $\gcd(x,y)+y$. It is a well-known fact that $\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(a-b,b)$ for $a\geq b$. Applying it to our formula, we get $\gcd(x-y,y)+y$.

Using the fact that $\gcd(x-y,y)\le x-y$, we get $\gcd(x-y,y)+y\le x-y+y=x$. Hence, $\gcd(x,y)+y\le x$ for $1\le y \lt x$.

For $y=x-1$, we have $\gcd(x,x-1)+x-1=1+x-1=x$, which is the maximal possible value.

Note that the constraints allow finding the optimal $y$ in $O(x)$, while the above solution works in $O(1)$.
